newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices slide as U.S. heating oil stocks rise.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices slide as U.S. heating oil stocks rise.

text.p: World oil prices shed more gains on Wednesday as the dizzying rally which took crude to six-year highs unwound further under growing supplies of winter heating oil in the United States.
London futures for bellwether North Sea Brent crude on Wednesday morning was trading 30 cents down at $23.48 a barrel.
Dealers said prices may have peaked for the time being but that it was too early to predict an end to the bull run which two weeks ago carried Brent above $25 a barrel.
"I don't think we can write this market off yet -- it's far too early in the winter," said Russell Hill, senior crude trader at Austrian oil company OMV in London.
"It's not the end of the bull market but it has been severely tested."
Crude came under selling pressure on Wednesday after latest weekly U.S. data showing a build in stocks of heating oil.
The American Petroleum Institute (API) said stocks of distillates (heating oil and diesel) showed a 3.6 million barrel build to nearly 118 million barrels.
Heating oil stocks in the key U.S. northeast region rose 2.8 million barrels.

Although the region -- the world's largest heating oil market -- is still 14.7 million barrels (34 percent) short of last year's stock levels, traders said the gap was expected to close further as oil flows north from Refinery Row on the U.S. Gulf.
"It looks pretty bearish for heating oil, which has been driving the market, so I think it could bring the whole energy complex down," a East Coast U.S. trader said.
U.S. Gulf refineries have cranked out record volumes of heating oil to meet rampant demand for replenishing low stocks.
"Distillates in the U.S. are looking more comfortable and output is up, but they're squeezing a dry sponge. There's very little if any extra capacity," said Hill at OMV.
U.S. Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary said on Tuesday production of distillates had shot through the roof.
"Producers have been standing on their in the last four to five weeks to keep up with demand."
O'Leary met with a number of oil executives recently in an effort to combat historically low levels of distillates stocks.
She said short-term efforts by the U.S. refining industry to open more pipeline space and curtail planned maintenance for some crude units had boosted stocks.
But inventories remained vulnerable to sustained cold weather spells, she said.
Winter weather his year in the U.S. is likely to prove slightly colder than normal, a leading meteorologist said on Monday.

A colder and weaker than normal jet stream from the Pacific Ocean was likely to keep temperatures below average, said Jon Davis, chief meteorologist at brokerage Smith Barney. Crude oil prices in dollars per barrel:
